source_read: PDF, pp. 298-306 (all pages, born-digital text layer; Tables 2 and 3 and every number used checked on pages rendered at 150 and 300 dpi)

claims.overstatement: Accurate overall, with four wording corrections. (1) 'with no stated selection rules' is not right: the review states broad inclusion rules (publications where cannabis was believed to have contributed to an emergency admission for a cardiovascular event or to the death; epidemiological studies designed to examine a link), searched PubMed and Scopus with listed keywords; what it lacks is search dates, counts and any appraisal, and its tables present a selection of publications. Suggested: with broad inclusion rules, no search dates and no appraisal. (2) The claim's wording that no minimum blood THC level can show cause hardens the review's hedge: it says minimum causal concentrations may not be possible to give because of delays from death to sampling. (3) CARDIA: no association with cardiovascular-disease mortality (not heart disease alone), in adults aged 18-30 followed for more than 25 years. (4) The firm recommendation (at least a contributory cause) is in the abstract; the discussion words the same step tentatively (arguably sufficient; not unreasonable), and the conclusion says such inclusion should be encouraged, so the claim's verb recommend is fair. The editors' closing inference (counting cannabis as a cause on these criteria would rest on THC being present plus the circumstances) matches the review's own criteria on p. 304.
claims.note: All numbers reproduce: 13 men aged 17-52, median 37 (recomputed from Table 2: same); blood THC in 8 cases 1.9-22 ng/mL (the text rounds to 2-22 and gives a median of 4, but the eight Table 2 values give 4.5); alcohol 0.04% and 0.119%; two Casier cases died days after admission; Dines case had no autopsy; Tormey case urine positive with no THC in blood, coroner found cannabis a secondary cause. Relayed figures match Table 3 and the text as printed: 4.8 (2.9-9.5) and 1.7 (0.6-5.1), n = 3,882; HR 4.2 (1.2-14) and 2.5 (0.9-7.3), n = 1,913; CARDIA n = 5,113. The Mittleman interval is relayed as printed; the primary paper was not read and is worth checking (reader's recollection is a lower limit of 2.4, unverified). 'Eleven of twelve' check: in Table 3, 7 studies report a raised estimate or significant association (Petronis, Mittleman, Mukamal, Rumalla, Draz, Desai, DeFilippis), 1 a non-significant 29% higher mortality (Frost), 2 give counts with no comparison (Jouanjus, Dines), 1 no association (Reis/CARDIA) and 1 less atherosclerosis in people who used cannabis (Lee): at most 8 of 12 (editors' count), so the claim's statement is right. The review also relays a null finding the claim omits: no increase in overall in-hospital mortality with cannabis use among more than 2 million US myocardial-infarction admissions (Desai).

anchors.extracted: English-language publications on fatalities attributed to cannabis (not synthetic cannabinoids) searched in PubMed and Scopus with listed keywords, plus publications cited in them where relevant; included where cannabis was believed to have contributed to an emergency admission for a cardiovascular or related event or to the death, and epidemiological studies designed to examine a link with cardiovascular disease. No search dates, counts or appraisal; Tables 1-3 are titled as summaries of selected publications.

At least 13 deaths from a cardiovascular mechanism reported, called very likely an under-estimate of the true incidence (no data on missed deaths); with very recent use (within a few hours), positive blood THC and a possible cardiac or cerebrovascular cause, cannabis should be considered at least a contributory cause of sudden or unexpected death.

Six publications [50-55], 13 people aged 17-52 (median 37), all male; 8 with significant coronary atherosclerosis and/or other pathology (3 with thrombus, 2 enlarged hearts, at least 3 myocardial infarctions); 5 with little or no obvious pathology (17-42, mean 31, which Table 2 does not reproduce (editors' calculation: 29.0 or 32.8 depending on which case is counted)); case authors believed cannabis a significant contributor.

Bachs & Morland, 6 men 17-43, blood THC 22, 4, 2, 5 (alcohol 0.04%), 3 and 7 ng/mL; Tormey, 37, urine positive, no THC in blood, coroner found cannabis a secondary cause of death; Casier, 52 and 28, urine positive, died 3 days and a few days after admission; Hartung, 23 and 28, blood THC 5.2 and 1.9 ng/mL; Dines, 18, reported use, urine confirmed, no autopsy; Orsini, 40, urine positive, alcohol 0.119%, authors suggested a possible link. Blood THC in 8 (1.9-22 ng/mL), alcohol in 2.
8 deaths with blood THC 2-22 ng/mL (median 4); 4 urine positive for cannabinoids; 1 with no cannabinoid measurement; in all, recent use was regarded as the trigger and no other drugs were implicated.

Twelve epidemiological studies [53, 56-66]; the text says eleven showed trends to increased mortality or significant associations, but Table 3 supports at most 8 (editors' count; Reis/CARDIA null, Lee opposite, Jouanjus and Dines descriptive). Mittleman case-crossover, 3,882 people with myocardial infarction (1,258 women), 64 centres, 1989-1996: risk 4.8 (95% CI 2.9-9.5) in the hour after smoking cannabis and 1.7 (0.6-5.1) in the second hour; no toxicology to confirm THC.

Mukamal, inception cohort of 1,913 people hospitalized for myocardial infarction, 45 centres, 1989-1994: hazard ratio 4.2 (95% CI 1.2-14) for weekly use and 2.5 (0.9-7.3) for less than weekly. Reis (CARDIA), 5,113 adults aged 18-30 followed for more than 25 years, 84% reported use: cumulative lifetime and recent use not associated with cardiovascular-disease mortality.

More than 2 million US myocardial-infarction admissions (Desai): no increase in overall mortality with cannabis use. Two systematic reviews disagree: one [67] found an association with cardiovascular disease, stronger for ischaemic stroke (81 case reports with 116 people, 29 observational studies); the other [68] found no compelling evidence linking use with mortality.

Some deaths attributed to cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome [75-78], no details or numbers. The larger studies and systematic reviews leave the link with cardiovascular death unclear; symptoms could arise from other causes (channelopathies, tobacco); risk probably rare; ideally THC should be recorded in death statistics so as not to underestimate cannabis-associated mortality.

General criteria for inferring a drug death by excluding other causes: the drug can cause death, is present at a concentration able to do so, and fits the circumstances; for a sudden death without significant injury and with THC in blood, the authors judge it not unreasonable to include cannabis in the cause or part cause, especially with no other significant drugs present.

A coroner-commentary source [80] holds cannabis contributory only if used within 2 h of the arrest and ideally with THC confirmed in blood; most reports lacked a blood THC; a blood THC test, not urine cannabinoids or history alone, is needed to associate a death with recent use.

Because of delays from death to sampling, minimum causal THC concentrations may not be possible to give; most forensic laboratories detect 1-2 ng/mL in post-mortem blood and lower values could reflect use days earlier; with THC quantified and the criteria met, inclusion as causal or contributory could arguably be sufficient.
The authors argue that including cannabis as a cause or contributor in appropriate cases should be encouraged, to make burden-of-disease estimates reflect harm.
After smoking, blood THC falls below 10% of its peak within an hour and below 5 ng/mL within a few hours; effects depend on tolerance and on how soon after the event sampling is done.

key_findings.correction: Medians recomputed from Table 1: 26 for all 35 people (the one age printed as 40s does not affect it) and 35 for the five women (24, 33, 35, 36, 45); same as the card.
Median of the eight blood values recomputed: 4.5 ng/mL, same.
Values agree with Table 3 as printed. The relayed Mittleman lower limit (2.9) should be checked against the primary paper: see reporting issue 5.

Hedge lost: the authors say that, because of delays from death to sampling, it may not be possible to give minimum THC concentrations that might be regarded as causal (p. 304, Discussion paragraph 12), not that no minimum can be given. The same hardening recurs in the interpretation gap and the risk-of-bias reasoning (citable for their statement that no minimum post-mortem THC concentration can indicate cause). Rest confirmed.

reporting_issues.note: Same contradiction found independently in step 1.
Confirmed: in Table 2 all five deaths without a blood value had urine evidence (Tormey, the two Casier cases, Dines with urine confirmation in the circumstances column, Orsini).
Same finding in step 1 (at most 8 of 12 by a generous reading).

Log-scale check reproduced: 4.8 is 0.50 from 2.9 and 0.68 from 9.5. A lower limit of 2.4 would be symmetric (0.69), which matches this reader's unverified recollection of the primary paper (Mittleman et al., 2001); worth checking there before the 2.9 is used.

Recomputed: the five described by their findings (40, 42, 17, 28, 37) average 32.8; with the epilepsy case (18) instead of the case with an organizing thrombus (37) the mean is 29.0; neither gives the printed 31.

risk_of_bias.note: Agree with high overall and with the domains (undocumented selection, no appraisal, text summaries leaning towards a causal reading).

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial is right. One wording point: the gap statement says the authors hold that no minimum THC concentration can be given; they say it may not be possible (see key finding 8). Its remark that post-mortem changes in THC are not discussed is fair: the review names delays from death to sampling as the reason, without discussing redistribution or loss after death.

missed: p. 302, section 7, 4th paragraph: among more than 2 million US hospital admissions for myocardial infarction, no increase in overall mortality with cannabis use (Desai et al.), a second null finding on death that neither the review's count of eleven of twelve nor the card's key findings mention (Table 3 lists Desai only as a risk factor for myocardial infarction).

p. 306, reference 55: the title of Tormey's report (on misinterpretation of cannabis in a coroner's court) suggests the case author disputed the coroner's finding that cannabis was a secondary cause; if so, this death was linked to cannabis by the coroner, not by the case author. To check in the primary report, which was not read.
